content: 1. In patients with vascular disease, the dose of ribavirin (RBV) must be reduced if hemoglobin (Hb) levels decrease by ≥2 g/dL within any 4-week period. If, after 4 weeks on a reduced dose, the Hb remains below 12 g/dL, combination therapy should be discontinued. 2. For patients with renal failure, RBV dosing must be adjusted. Those with a creatinine clearance of <50 mL/min should not be treated with RBV. Patients on dialysis should have their RBV dose reduced to 200 mg per day or administered three times per week. Increased monitoring is required for this group. 3. In patients with end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance 20–40 mL/min), a starting dose of pegylated interferon alpha-2a (PEG-IFN α2a) at 135 μg once weekly is recommended. 4. Treatment recommendations, including stopping rules and efficacy monitoring, are detailed in Appendix 5 for individuals with genotype 1 HCV infection receiving PEG-IFN/RBV and either boceprevir or telaprevir. Extended treatment regimens may be considered for slow virological responders and individuals with HIV or cirrhosis. 5. In the PRESCO study, higher weight-based RBV dosing and extended treatment duration (from 48 to 72 weeks) were used, resulting in improved outcomes but with a higher risk of severe anemia. 6. For genotype 2/3 infections, extending treatment duration from 24 to 48 weeks resulted in a higher sustained virological response (SVR) rate (82% vs. 67%). 7. The duration of PEG-IFN and RBV therapy for genotypes 2, 3, 5, and 6 varies based on treatment response. If the viral load decreases by less than 2 logs at 12 weeks or remains detectable at 24 weeks, treatment should be stopped. 8. An extended rapid virological response (eRVR) is associated with a high likelihood of achieving SVR. For patients with a baseline viral load <400,000–800,000 IU/mL, a reduced treatment duration of 24 weeks may be considered. 9. Conversely, for patients with a slow virological response (detectable viral load at 12 weeks with a ≥2 log drop and a negative viral load at 24 weeks), a prolonged 72-week course of therapy may be considered. 10. Special considerations are required for specific populations, including people who inject drugs (PWID), individuals co-infected with HIV, children, adolescents, and those with cirrhosis. Care for PWID should emphasize respect, non-discrimination, and additional adherence and psychological support as needed. 11. Targeted HCV screening is recommended for PWID due to their high prevalence of infection. Repeated screening is necessary for individuals at ongoing risk, and reinfection after successful treatment or spontaneous clearance should be considered. 12. HCV case-finding and treatment within specialist drug dependency services have been shown to be cost-effective in high-income settings. Screening for HBV and HIV is also recommended in PWID. 13. Treatment of HCV in PWID requires integrated services to address other healthcare needs, including opioid dependency, alcohol excess, and harm reduction strategies to prevent acquisition of other bloodborne viruses like HBV and HIV. 14. Avoidance of discrimination and stigmatization of PWID is essential. Care should only be provided with informed consent. Needle and syringe programs should provide sterile equipment with low dead space, and peer interventions may help reduce the incidence of viral hepatitis. 15. HCV treatment in PWID is both efficacious and cost-effective. WHO recommends that all adults and children with chronic HCV infection, including PWID, be assessed for antiviral treatment. 16. Methadone levels may decrease in individuals treated with PEG-IFN/RBV. Although this interaction is usually subclinical, monitoring for withdrawal symptoms is recommended. 17. HIV and HCV co-infection poses challenges due to the negative impact of HIV on HCV progression and the therapeutic complexities of drug interactions. Treatment should be managed by clinicians experienced in both infections. 18. In HIV/HCV co-infected individuals, HCV treatment may slow hepatic fibrosis progression and delay the onset of decompensated cirrhosis. HCV treatment is a priority in this population. 19. Clinical stabilization of HIV with antiretroviral therapy (ART) is advisable before initiating HCV treatment, particularly in individuals with advanced immunosuppression (CD4 count <200 cells/mm³). ART initiation may be delayed until CD4 counts improve. 20. HCV infection in HIV co-infected individuals can be treated with PEG-IFN/RBV, with or without direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) like boceprevir, telaprevir, simeprevir, or sofosbuvir, depending on the genotype. 21. Special consideration is required for selecting ART regimens in HIV/HCV co-infected individuals to avoid drug interactions and overlapping toxicities. Elevated bilirubin levels are common with sofosbuvir and atazanavir. 22. ART should be initiated in all individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. ART is also recommended for individuals with CD4 counts between 350 and 500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage. 23. For children under five years of age with HIV, ART should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. Pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should start a triple antiretroviral regimen for the duration of the risk of mother-to-child transmission. 24. First-line ART regimens for adults and adolescents include tenofovir (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) + efavirenz (EFV) as a fixed-dose combination. Alternative regimens include zidovudine (AZT) + 3TC + EFV or nevirapine (NVP). 25. For children, preferred regimens vary by age. For those under three years, abacavir (ABC) or AZT + 3TC + lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) is recommended. For children aged three years or older, ABC + 3TC + EFV is preferred. 26. The use of stavudine (d4T) in first-line regimens should be discontinued due to its metabolic toxicities. Its use should be restricted to special cases where other antiretrovirals cannot be used and for the shortest duration possible. 27. ART-induced hepatotoxicity is a concern in HIV/HCV co-infected individuals, but the benefits of ART generally outweigh the risks. Liver enzymes (ALT and AST) should be monitored at one month after ART initiation and every 3–6 months thereafter. 28. Careful consideration of drug interactions is essential to avoid toxicity, ensure regimen efficacy, and prevent the development of antiretroviral resistance. Weight-based dosing and dose adjustments of RBV are recommended in some cases.
